q: What are the two files that EZGmail needs before a program can reach Gmail?
options: A credentials file that identifies the program and a token file that records the owner's permission
A username file and a password file that the program reads at every start
A certificate file and a log file that Google writes after every sent message
A contacts file and a labels file that are downloaded from the Gmail website
why: The credentials file is made once in the Google Cloud console and the token file records the permission the owner gave.

q: Why must the token file be kept private?
options: It is large, and a public copy would slow down every program that reads it
It works like a password: whoever holds it can use the owner's Gmail through the program
It holds the text of all sent mail, which Gmail would delete if it were shared
It expires the moment a second person looks at it, so it must stay unread
why: The token records the owner's permission, so anyone with the file acts with that permission.

q: What does a dry run change in a program that sends or deletes mail?
options: The program is run twice, and only the second run sends the mail
The mail is sent but marked as a test so that the recipient ignores it
The line that sends or deletes is replaced by a print, so nothing real is touched
The program waits until the owner confirms each message by hand
why: A dry run prints what would be done and leaves the real mailbox alone.

q: What does this program print?
options: DRY RUN: done
SENT: done
None
DONE
why: With send left as None the function returns the DRY RUN text; the second call would pass send and return what send returns.

q: What does one call of the send function need to give, and what does the library build from it?
options: The recipient, subject and body; the library builds a text message with those header fields and hands it to the Gmail API
Only the body; the library asks for the recipient and subject while it runs
The recipient and a file name; the library reads the body from that file
A finished MIME text that the library sends without looking at it
why: send takes recipient, subject and body, and the message with its To and Subject fields is built for the caller.

q: What does this program print?

text/plain
multipart/mixed
text/plain Subject line
why: MIMEText with the subtype plain has the content type text/plain, and the header fields are set like dictionary entries.

q: What happens to the message when files are named as attachments?
options: It stays a single text message and the files are pasted into the body
It is split into one separate message for each file
It becomes a multipart message: the text is the first part and each file is a further part carrying the file's name
It is sent as HTML so that the files can be shown as links
why: A message with attachments is multipart, with the text first and one part per file.

print(len(list(m.walk())))
why: walk() yields the container (multipart/mixed), the text part and the attachment part: three.

q: In what form are the cc and bcc arguments given to the send function?
options: As strings of comma-separated addresses that become header fields of the message
As lists of contact names that Gmail looks up in the address book
As numbers that count how many extra copies are sent
As file names of text files that hold one address per line

q: How does a program send a body that is HTML?

It wraps the body in angle brackets and leaves the subtype alone
It gives the subtype as 'html'; the default is 'plain' and any other string is refused
It sends the body twice, once as plain text and once as HTML
why: mimeSubtype is plain by default and html makes the body HTML.

html

q: What do ezgmail.unread(), recent() and search() return?

Single messages, each holding the list of its replies
Only the subject lines of the matching mail
The number of matching messages as one integer

options: Five threads, each holding one message
One thread, whose list holds five message objects
Five threads, each holding all five messages
No thread, because only single messages can be searched
why: The unit of the result is the conversation: one thread with its messages inside.

The owner attribute; it keeps the phone number

The reply attribute; it keeps the address of the last reply

It asks the owner whether to keep the old file
It saves the new one under a name with a number added
It appends the new content after the old content

smtplib, with port 25 for a plain connection and 465 for an encrypted one

q: What does send_message do with the Bcc field of the message?
options: It sends the Bcc field to every recipient so that all can see it
It ignores the Bcc recipients and sends only to To and Cc
It sends to the Bcc recipients but leaves the Bcc field out of the text that is sent
It refuses the message because Bcc fields are not allowed

q: A message has To, Cc and Bcc fields. Which statement about the delivery is right?
options: Only the To recipients are read from the message; the others must be listed again
The Cc and Bcc recipients are read, but the Bcc field is shown to the To recipient
The Bcc field is the only one read, and the others are ignored
The sender and all three kinds of recipient come from the message; the Bcc recipients get a copy that does not show the Bcc field
why: send_message reads From, To, Cc and Bcc and removes Bcc from the sent text.

email.mime.text.MIMEText, because it is the newest
email.header.Header, which holds a whole message

The higher priority of gateway texts, which wakes the owner too often

The service encrypts only topics with random names
Anyone may publish to a topic and anyone may subscribe, so the name is the only protection and is treated like a password
A topic name must be unique for each message

The complete mailbox, split into several messages
